open_vagueness.text: Whether the opportunistic sweep should be bounded by count (reap at most N records per invocation) or by time (spend at most Nms), and what that bound is. Both keep 'page open' fast; a count bound is deterministic and testable, a time bound degrades gracefully on a slow filesystem.

Whether --site is worth its cost at all in this slice. It is the only ask requiring a new persisted record field (c15) and a privacy decision (c16); --older-than and --status filters need neither and cover the reported symptom. Deferring --site to a follow-up would let this ship without touching what a session record retains.
open_vagueness.resolution: --site stays in this slice. The user confirmed it, and the visited-host field it needs is no longer a cost carried by --site alone: the same field is what repetition-mapping (c23) matches on.

open_vagueness.text: Whether non-Linux hosts are in scope for the sweep. terminate_pid uses os.kill/SIGTERM/SIGKILL and _locked uses fcntl.flock (session_store.py:290-327, 696-708) — both POSIX-only, and the store is already Linux-shaped before this change. The sweep does not make it worse, but automating process termination raises the cost of the assumption if it is ever wrong.

How two concurrent webglass invocations are distinguished, given _DEFAULT_CALLER = 'cli' is hardcoded for all of them (c29). Blocking because c24's caller-scoped sweep and c23's caller-scoped reuse are both unsafe under the current identity model: the sweep would reap a sibling process's sessions and reuse could hand over another task's session. Candidates: derive caller from the OS process, require an explicit --caller/--task, or scope both to ids minted by this process.
open_vagueness.resolution: Identity follows the Playwright-MCP model: a session belongs to the client/process that opened it, and that owner — not the literal 'cli' caller string — is what scopes both the sweep (c24) and reuse (c23). An invocation may only reap or reuse sessions its own owner opened; another owner's sessions are invisible to it, exactly as one MCP server instance cannot touch another's browser.
